provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: Art: still life drawing
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to state the importance of light and shadow in still life drawing.
The pupils should be able to draw a simple still life arrangement.

Introduction:
Today we will learn about still life drawing. Last term we practiced drawing basic shapes.

Content:
Still life drawing is drawing objects that do not move. We use everyday objects like mangoes, bottles and plates. Light and shadow make drawing look real. Light shows where the sun shines. Shadow shows where light cannot reach. When drawing still life, first draw the outline of objects. Then add light and shadow. For example, if you draw a basket of oranges, the side facing the window will be light. The other side will have shadow.

Class activity:
Each pupil will arrange three fruits on a table. They will draw the arrangement and shade it with light and shadow.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is still life drawing?
2. Name two objects you can draw for still life.
3. How does shadow help in drawing?
4. Why do artists use light in drawing?

Summary:
Still life drawing teaches us to draw objects that do not move with proper light and shadow.

topics.title: Music: staff notation
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to identify the lines and spaces on the staff.
The pupils should be able to read and play simple notes.

Introduction:
Today we will learn about staff notation. Last week we learned about different types of musical notes.

Content:
Staff notation is a way to write music. It has five lines and four spaces. Each line and space represents a different musical note. The lines are E, G, B, D, F from bottom to top. The spaces are F, A, C, E from bottom to top. We use a clef to show which notes to play. The treble clef is for higher notes. The bass clef is for lower notes. For example, in a Nigerian folk song like 'Sakara', staff notation helps us write the exact notes to play.

Class activity:
Pupils will draw a staff and label the lines and spaces. They will then practice reading simple notes written on the staff.

Evaluation questions:
1. How many lines are on the music staff?
2. Name the notes on the lines of the treble clef.
3. What is the purpose of staff notation?
4. How many spaces are on the music staff?

Summary:
Staff notation helps us read and write music accurately using lines and spaces.

topics.title: Art: perspective
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to explain one point perspective.
The pupils should be able to draw a street using one point perspective.

Introduction:
Today we will learn about perspective in art. Last week we practiced still life drawing.

Content:
Perspective makes drawings look three-dimensional. One point perspective uses one vanishing point. All lines in the drawing go to this point. For example, when drawing a street, the road and buildings appear to get smaller as they go into the distance. The horizon line is where the sky meets the ground. The vanishing point is on the horizon line. In Lagos, when you look down a long street like Allen Avenue, it looks like it disappears at one point.

Class activity:
Pupils will draw a street scene using one point perspective. They will include buildings, road and horizon line.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is one point perspective?
2. Where is the vanishing point placed?
3. How does perspective make drawings look real?
4. What is the horizon line?

Summary:
One point perspective helps us create depth in drawings by using a single vanishing point.

topics.title: Music: Nigerian composers
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to identify works of Nigerian composers.
The pupils should be able to discuss their favourite piece of Nigerian music.

Introduction:
Today we will learn about Nigerian composers. Last week we learned about staff notation.

Content:
Nigerian composers create beautiful music using our cultural heritage. Fela Kuti is famous for Afrobeat music. He composed songs like 'Water No Get Enemy'. Ayo Bankole composed classical music with African themes. He used instruments like talking drum in his compositions. Nigerian music often tells stories about our way of life. During harmattan season, some composers write songs about the cold weather and harvest time.

Class activity:
Pupils will listen to pieces by Nigerian composers and discuss what they like about each piece.

Evaluation questions:
1. Name one Nigerian composer.
2. What type of music is Fela Kuti famous for?
3. How does Nigerian music reflect our culture?
4. Why do composers write about seasons like harmattan?

Summary:
Nigerian composers create music that tells our stories and shows our cultural heritage.

topics.title: Art: sculpture in the round
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to create a clay figure on an armature.
The pupils should be able to finish and display a sculpture.

Introduction:
Today we will learn about sculpture in the round. Last week we practiced perspective drawing.

Content:
Sculpture in the round is a sculpture you can walk around and see from all sides. We use clay to make these sculptures. An armature is a support structure for the sculpture. We can use wire or sticks to make the armature. For example, when making a clay figure of a market woman, we first make a wire frame. Then we add clay to form the body. We smooth the clay and add details like the face and clothes. Finally, we let it dry and paint it with bright colours.

Class activity:
Pupils will create a simple clay figure on a wire armature. They will finish and display their sculptures.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is sculpture in the round?
2. What is an armature used for?
3. What material do we use for sculpture in the round?
4. How do you make a sculpture look like a market woman?

Summary:
Sculpture in the round allows us to create three-dimensional figures we can view from all sides.

topics.title: Drama: play production
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to participate in auditions and take on roles.
The pupils should be able to rehearse for a play.

Introduction:
Today we will start working on a play production. Last term we learned about different types of plays.

Content:
Play production means putting on a play for an audience. First, we need to choose a story. It could be a folk tale like 'The Tortoise and the Birds'. Then we audition pupils for different roles. Each pupil will practice their part. Rehearsal means practicing the play many times. We need to remember our lines and movements. We also need to think about costumes and props. For example, if we are doing a play about market day, we can use baskets and fake money as props.

Class activity:
The class will audition for different roles in a short play about market day. Pupils will then rehearse their parts.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is play production?
2. What happens during auditions?
3. Why do we need to rehearse a play?
4. What are props in a play?

Summary:
Play production involves choosing a story, assigning roles and rehearsing for a performance.

topics.title: Art: batik
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to explain the process of making batik.
The pupils should be able to create a batik design.

Introduction:
Today we will learn about batik art. Last week we worked on a play production.

Content:
Batik is a traditional way of making designs on cloth. We use wax and dye to create beautiful patterns. First, we draw a design on cloth with wax. The wax acts as a resist. Then we put the cloth in dye. The dye only sticks where there is no wax. After dyeing, we boil the cloth to remove the wax. This shows our design. In Nigeria, batik is used to make beautiful clothes like agbada and gele. Common patterns include geometric shapes and traditional symbols.

Class activity:
Pupils will create a simple batik design on a small piece of cloth using wax and dye.

Evaluation questions:
1. What materials do we use for batik?
2. What does the wax do in batik making?
3. How do we remove the wax after dyeing?
4. Name one traditional Nigerian garment made with batik.

Summary:
Batik is a traditional art form that uses wax and dye to create beautiful patterns on cloth.

topics.title: Music: recorder or voice
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to learn a simple melody on recorder or with their voice.
The pupils should be able to perform in pairs.

Introduction:
Today we will learn music using recorder or our voices. Last week we learned about batik art.

Content:
The recorder is a musical instrument we blow into to make sounds. We can also use our voices to sing. To play recorder, we cover different holes with our fingers to make different notes. We can learn simple melodies like 'Twinkle Twinkle Little Star'. When we perform in pairs, one person can play while the other sings. Or we can play different parts together. In Nigerian music, we often call and respond. One person sings a line and another answers.

Class activity:
Pupils will learn a simple Nigerian folk song on recorder or with their voices. They will then perform in pairs.

Evaluation questions:
1. How do you make sound on a recorder?
2. What is a simple melody we can learn?
3. How do we perform in pairs?
4. What is call and response in music?

Summary:
We can make music using recorders or our voices by learning simple melodies and performing together.

topics.title: Dance: cultural ballet
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to choreograph a simple cultural ballet piece.
The pupils should be able to plan costumes for a cultural dance.

Introduction:
Today we will learn about cultural ballet. Last week we performed music in pairs.

Content:
Cultural ballet combines traditional dance with ballet techniques. We create movements that tell our stories. For example, we can dance movements that show farming or market activities. Choreography means planning the dance steps. We need to think about timing and formations. Costumes are important for cultural ballet. They show our traditions. For example, we can use Ankara fabric to make dresses that reflect our cultural heritage. We can also use beads and cowrie shells to decorate.

Class activity:
Pupils will work in groups to choreograph a short cultural ballet piece about a Nigerian festival. They will also plan simple costumes.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is cultural ballet?
2. What is choreography?
3. Why are costumes important in cultural ballet?
4. What type of fabric can we use for cultural ballet costumes?

Summary:
Cultural ballet combines traditional dance with ballet techniques to tell our stories through movement.

topics.title: Revision and showcase
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to display their art works.
The pupils should be able to perform in a class concert.

Introduction:
Today we will revise what we learned and showcase our works. This term we learned about art, music and dance.

Content:
In our revision, we will remember all the things we learned. We practiced still life drawing, staff notation, perspective, sculpture, batik and cultural ballet. Now we will show our best works. For art, we can display our drawings, sculptures and batik designs. For music, we can play recorder or sing our learned songs. For dance, we can perform our cultural ballet pieces. This is like a small exhibition and concert. We can invite other classes to see our work.

Class activity:
The class will set up an exhibition of their art works. They will also prepare for a class concert where they perform music and dance pieces.

Evaluation questions:
1. What art work are you most proud of this term?
2. What song did you learn to play or sing?
3. What cultural ballet piece did your group create?
4. How do you feel about showcasing your work?

Summary:
We will display our art works and perform in a class concert to celebrate what we learned this term.
